title: Google open-sources HEIR, a compiler that runs AI inference on encrypted data the server never decrypts
subtitle: The MLIR-based toolchain converts trained TensorFlow models into fully homomorphic-encryption versions, closing one of the longest-standing gaps between the FHE research community and practical deployment.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google published HEIR — Homomorphic Encryption Intermediate Representation — on August 14, an MLIR-based compiler toolchain that takes a trained TensorFlow model and rewrites it to run inference on encrypted inputs using fully homomorphic encryption. The server executing the model never sees plaintext; the client sends ciphertext, the model computes on ciphertext, the client decrypts the result. The project ships under Apache 2.0 with two backend targets — OpenFHE and Lattigo — a Python package for common cases, and a companion paper on arXiv.

Fully homomorphic encryption has worked in theory since 2009 but has been useless at practical scale — the ciphertext blow-up and layer-by-layer bootstrapping made a single forward pass through even a small vision model take hours. HEIR is not the first FHE compiler, but it is the first to combine a TensorFlow front-end that a normal ML engineer can use with the layered optimization passes — ciphertext packing, parameter selection, arithmetization — that specialists spent the last five years hand-coding. Google's blog post frames it as lowering the barrier to entry; the arXiv companion paper is more direct about the underlying gains in throughput.

The audiences that care most are healthcare, finance, and government — anywhere the compliance regime forbids sending raw customer data to an inference API. HEIR does not make that use case free — encrypted inference remains orders of magnitude slower than plaintext — but it makes the toolchain accessible enough that a hospital or a bank can pilot without hiring a cryptography team. It also lands into a policy environment where the EU AI Act's high-risk provisions took effect on August 2, and where the FTC has signaled it will use existing deception authority to police undisclosed data flows.

Takeaway for learners: privacy-preserving ML is about to stop being a niche. For a decade it was a research subfield with a handful of practitioners; a TensorFlow-to-FHE compiler with a real backend and an open license changes that. If you have a systems or ML-engineering background, working through the HEIR examples this week gets you in front of a wave that most job listings do not yet know how to describe — and that is usually the best time to arrive.
